L7B  /  Pathological basis of oral & systemic disease

Neoplasia — Part 2

Pathogenesis and the hallmarks of cancer. How a normal cell becomes autonomous — oncogenes, tumour suppressors, p53 — and the eight capabilities every cancer must acquire.

Lecturer
Dr Joseph Ryan
Sections
15
Core reading
Underwood’s Ch. 5
Key paper
Hanahan & Weinberg 2011
01

Neoplastic transformation

Two kinds of change, and what turns a neoplasm malignant.

Change 1

Genetic alterations

Mutations, deletions, translocations, rearrangements, amplifications.

Change 2

Epigenetic changes

e.g. promoter methylation silencing transcription — the DNA sequence is unchanged, but the gene is switched off.

Malignant transformation

Neoplasms acquiring further characteristics: invasion and metastases.

Two separate events

Neoplastic transformation makes a cell autonomous. Malignant transformation adds invasion and metastasis on top. A benign neoplasm has undergone the first without the second — which is why some benign lesions can later progress, as an adenomatous polyp does to adenocarcinoma.

02

Initiation, promotion, progression

Three defined stages, and the vocabulary around them.

  1. Initiation
    A carcinogen induces the genetic alteration(s) that give(s) the transformed cell its neoplastic potential.
  2. Promotion
    The stimulation of clonal proliferation of the initiated transformed cell.
  3. Progression
    The process culminating in malignant behaviour.
TermMeaning
ClonalOriginating from single cells that have become transformed by cumulative mutational events, such as in neoplasms
PolyclonalOriginating from multiple cells
CarcinogenAn environmental agent participating in the causation of tumours
Multistep carcinogenesisThe hypothesis that cancer requires an accumulation of several successive changes, not one
Why does calling neoplasms "clonal" matter?

Because it says the tumour originates from a single cell that became transformed by cumulative mutational events — not from many cells transforming in parallel. Every cell in the tumour therefore inherits that founder's alterations, which is what makes molecular markers and targeted therapy possible, and it fits the multistep carcinogenesis hypothesis: successive changes accumulating in one lineage.

From the lecture slides
03

Genetic mechanisms in carcinogenesis

Three routes to a transformed cell.

Route 1

Expression of telomerase

Restoring the ability to divide indefinitely.

Route 2

Loss of a tumour suppressor

Loss or inactivation of both copies of a tumour suppressor gene.

Route 3

Oncogene activation

Activation or abnormal expression of oncogenes.

Note the asymmetry — it is examinable

Tumour suppressors need both copies lost (recessive at cell level). Oncogenes need only one activated allele (dominant at cell level). Brakes must both fail; one stuck accelerator is enough.

From the lecture slides
04

Tumour suppressor genes

The two-hit model, and two functional classes.

The double-hit model

The first ‘hit’ is the acquired mutational loss of function or inheritance of a defective (mutant) allele of a tumour suppressor gene, the other allele being normal (wild type) and expressing sufficient suppressive effect.

The second ‘hit’ is the acquired mutational loss of function of the normal allele, thus now fully depriving the cell of the suppressive effect of that tumour suppressor.

Why inherited cancer syndromes exist

Someone born with one defective allele already carries the first hit in every cell. They need only one further event, in any single cell, rather than two in the same cell — which is why familial cancers present earlier and often multifocally.

Two functional classes

Class 1

Caretaker genes

Maintain the integrity of the genome by repairing DNA damage.

Class 2

Gatekeeper genes

Inhibit the proliferation or promote the death of cells with damaged DNA.

A way to hold the pair

A caretaker fixes the damage. A gatekeeper decides whether a damaged cell is allowed through — arrest, or apoptosis. Lose caretakers and mutations accumulate; lose gatekeepers and mutated cells are permitted to divide.

From the lecture slides
05

p53: the guardian of the genome

The most frequently mutated gene in human cancer.

The tumour suppressor gene p53, situated on the short arm of chromosome 17, is the gene most frequently mutated and extensively studied in human cancer. Normally it:

  1. Repairs damaged DNA before S phase
    By arresting the cell cycle in G1 until the damage is repaired.
  2. Induces apoptotic cell death
    If there is extensive DNA damage.

Mechanisms of p53 loss of function

MutationsEither rendering the gene unreadable (nonsense mutations) or encoding a defective protein or protein with altered function (missense mutations)
Dominant-negative complexesComplexes of normal p53 and mutant p53 proteins (in heterozygous individuals or cells) inactivating or subverting the function of the normal protein — an exception to the two-hit model
Viral protein bindingBinding of normal p53 protein to proteins encoded by oncogenic DNA viruses (e.g. human papillomavirus, polyomaviruses)
The exception matters

Mutant p53 can poison the normal protein it partners with. That means one mutated allele can be enough — an explicit exception to the two-hit model. If a question asks when a single hit suffices for a tumour suppressor, this is the answer.

Straight to Lecture 6 and L7C

The third mechanism is how HPV causes cancer: viral E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates pRb. The virus does not need to mutate anything — it disables the proteins directly. That is the link between the oropharyngeal cancer statistics in Lecture 6 and the molecular machinery here.

How can a single mutated p53 allele cause loss of p53 function, when the two-hit model requires both?

Through a dominant-negative effect: complexes of normal and mutant p53 protein form in heterozygous cells, and the mutant subunit inactivates or subverts the function of the normal protein. The lecture flags this explicitly as an exception to the two-hit model. p53 function can also be lost without mutation at all, when oncogenic DNA viruses such as HPV bind and inactivate the normal protein.

From the lecture slides
06

Genomic instability

Losing the ability to notice damage.

Genomic instability

Cells that have lost the mechanisms for preserving genomic integrity by sensing and repairing DNA damage are said to have genomic instability.

Pattern 1

Chromosomal instability

Causing chromosome breaks — e.g. Fanconi anaemia.

Pattern 2

Microsatellite instability

Due to defective DNA mismatch repair — e.g. hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer.

Inherited DNA repair defects

Individuals born with inherited defects in DNA repair genes are at greatly increased risk for the development of cancer.

HNPCC syndromeFamilial carcinomas of the colon affecting predominantly the caecum and proximal colon; results from defects in genes involved in DNA mismatch repair
Xeroderma pigmentosumAn autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in DNA repair, associated with a greatly increased risk for cancers arising in sun-exposed skin
Genomic instability is an enabling characteristic

It does not itself drive growth. It accelerates the accumulation of the mutations that do — which is why the Hallmarks framework lists it separately as an enabling characteristic rather than a hallmark.

07

Oncogenes

Genes driving neoplastic behaviour, and how they are switched on.

Oncogenes are genes driving the neoplastic behaviour of cells.

Two routes to activation

Route 1

Altered protein

Mutations resulting in an oncoprotein molecule altered in such a way that it is excessively active.

Route 2

Too much normal protein

Excessive production of a normal oncoprotein.

Classification by function of the oncoprotein

FunctionExample
Growth factorssis — coding for platelet-derived growth factor
Receptors for growth factorserbB — coding for epidermal growth factor receptor
Signalling mediator with tyrosine kinase activitysrc
Signalling mediator with nucleotide binding activity, disrupting intracellular signallingras (and GTP)
Nuclear-binding transcription factor oncoproteins involved in the regulation of cellular proliferationmyc
The classification follows the signalling pathway

Read the five rows in order and they trace a signal from outside the cell to the nucleus: growth factor → receptor → membrane kinase → intracellular transducer → transcription factor. An oncogene can hijack the pathway at any point — and that is also the order of the normal proliferation sequence below.

The normal process of cell proliferation

  1. Binding of a growth factor
    To its specific receptor on the cell membrane.
  2. Receptor activation
    Transient and limited activation of the growth factor receptor, which in turn activates several signal-transducing proteins on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
  3. Signal transmission to the nucleus
    Transmission of the transduced signal across the cytosol.
  4. Nuclear regulatory factors
    Induction and activation of nuclear regulatory factors that initiate and regulate DNA transcription and the biosynthesis of other cellular components needed for cell division — organelles, membrane components, ribosomes.
  5. Cell cycle entry
    Entry and progression of the cell into the cell cycle.

Detecting oncogene activation

More oncoprotein within or on the cells Increased mRNA transcripts Increased gene copy number
The word “transient” in step 2

Normal receptor activation is transient and limited. Cancer converts that into continuous signalling — which is precisely Hallmark 1 below.

08

Epigenetic contributions

Changing expression without changing sequence.

MechanismEffect
Promoter hypermethylationGene silencing by hypermethylation of promoter DNA sequences, particularly at CpG islands in promoters
Histone modificationGene up- or down-regulation due to histone modifications (methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation) — the “histone code”
microRNAInterference with gene transcription by microRNA (short sequences of inhibitory RNA). Increased miRNA leads to more degradation of mRNA and reduced expression; decreased miRNA can enhance expression
Copy number changesTo enhancer and regulatory regions
Why silencing is as good as deleting

A tumour suppressor whose promoter is hypermethylated is intact but unread. The cell is just as unprotected as if the gene were deleted — but because the sequence is normal, sequencing alone would miss it. Epigenetic silencing is also, in principle, reversible, which is why it is a drug target.

09

The hallmarks of cancer

Hanahan and Weinberg's eight — the organising framework.

#HallmarkIn one line
1Self-sufficiency in growth signalsMakes its own accelerator
2Insensitivity to growth inhibitory signalsIgnores the brakes
3Altered cellular metabolismRefuels for building, not just energy
4Evasion of cell deathRefuses to die
5Unlimited replicative potentialNever ages out
6Sustained angiogenesisBuilds its own supply lines
7Invasion and metastasisLeaves home
8Evasion of immune surveillanceHides from the immune system

Plus two enabling characteristics: genomic instability and tumour-promoting inflammation.

From the lecture slides
10

Hallmarks 1 and 2: the accelerator and the brakes

Growth signal self-sufficiency, and insensitivity to inhibition.

1. Self-sufficiency in growth signals

Generally stems from gain-of-function mutations that convert proto-oncogenes to oncogenes. Cancer cells may:

  • Secrete their own growth factors, or induce stromal cells to produce growth factors in the tumour microenvironment
  • Overexpress or mutate growth factor receptors, which then function as oncoproteins
  • Acquire growth autonomy through mutations in genes encoding components of signalling pathways downstream of growth factor receptors
  • Show inappropriate and continuous stimulation of nuclear transcription factors that drive the expression of growth-promoting genes

Cell-cycle deregulation

There are two main cell cycle checkpoints, one at the G1/S transition and the other at G2/M, each tightly regulated by a balance of growth-promoting and growth-suppressing factors, as well as by sensors of DNA damage.

Gain-of-function mutations involving CDK4 or D cyclins Loss-of-function mutations involving CDKIs

2. Insensitivity to growth inhibitory signals

RBA key negative regulator of the cell cycle, directly or indirectly inactivated in most human cancers. Its function is to regulate the G1/S checkpoint — the portal through which cells must pass before DNA replication commences
TP53The most commonly mutated gene in human cancer. p53-mediated cell cycle arrest may be considered the primordial response to DNA damage; it also drives p53-induced senescence and apoptosis of cells with irreversible DNA damage
Two numbers

At least one of the four key regulators of the cell cycle — p16, cyclin D, CDK4, RB — is mutated in most human cancers. And more than 70% of human cancers have a defect in TP53, with the remainder often having defects upstream or downstream of it.

Why is the G1/S checkpoint the critical one for cancer?

Because it is the portal through which cells must pass before DNA replication commences. Once past it, damaged DNA gets copied into daughter cells. Both major gatekeepers act here: RB regulates the checkpoint directly, and p53 arrests the cycle in G1 until damage is repaired, or triggers apoptosis if it cannot be. Losing either lets damaged cells replicate.

From the lecture slides
11

Hallmarks 3, 4 and 5

Metabolism, cell death and replicative potential.

3. Altered cellular metabolism

Even in the presence of ample oxygen, cancer cells show a distinctive metabolism characterised by high levels of glucose uptake and increased conversion of glucose to lactate (fermentation) via the glycolytic pathway.

Why a cell would choose the inefficient route

Aerobic glycolysis provides rapidly dividing tumour cells with metabolic intermediates that are needed for the synthesis of cellular components, whereas mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation does not. A dividing cell needs building materials, not just ATP — and glycolysis supplies carbon skeletons. This is the Warburg effect.

The reprogramming is produced by signalling cascades downstream of growth factor receptors — the very same pathways that are deregulated by mutations in oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes. It is not a separate defect; it is a consequence of hallmarks 1 and 2.

4. Evasion of cell death

Tumour cells frequently contain mutations in genes that regulate apoptosis, making them resistant to cell death. Evasion occurs mainly through acquired mutations and changes in gene expression that disable key components of the intrinsic pathway, or that reset the balance of regulatory factors so as to favour cell survival in the face of intrinsic stresses.

5. Unlimited replicative potential

Loss of growth restraints is not enough — for indefinite growth, both cellular senescence and mitotic catastrophe must also be avoided.

Where telomerase fits

This is the hallmark that expression of telomerase from the genetic mechanisms section serves. Normal cells shorten their telomeres with each division and eventually senesce; re-expressing telomerase removes that counter.

12

Hallmarks 6, 7 and 8

Angiogenesis, spread, and hiding from immunity.

6. Sustained angiogenesis

The 1–2 mm limit

Even if a solid tumour possesses all of the genetic aberrations required for malignant transformation, it cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm in diameter unless it has the capacity to induce angiogenesis. In angiogenic tumours the balance between angiogenesis promoters and inhibitors is skewed in favour of promoters.

The same machinery as Lecture 4

Tumour angiogenesis uses the growth factors you met in healing — VEGF above all. A tumour recruits the wound-healing response to build its own blood supply, which is part of why chronic inflammation is tumour-promoting.

7. Invasion and metastasis

These are the major causes of cancer-related morbidity and mortality, and result from complex interactions involving cancer cells, stromal cells, and the extracellular matrix (ECM).

Tumour cells frequently escape their sites of origin and enter the circulation. The site at which metastases appear is related to two factors:

Factor 1

Anatomy

The anatomic location and vascular drainage of the primary tumour — where the blood goes first.

Factor 2

Tropism

The tropism of particular tumours for specific tissues — some tumours prefer certain destinations regardless of drainage.

8. Evasion of immune surveillance

  • Cancer cells express a variety of antigens that stimulate the host immune system
  • Despite that antigenicity, the immune response to established tumours is ineffective, and in some instances may actually promote cancer growth
  • Defining these mechanisms has led to effective new immunotherapies that work by reactivating latent host immune responses
Checkpoint blockade — PD-L1

The discovery of checkpoints that shut off anti-tumour immunity has led to the development of antibodies that block these checkpoints and release the brakes on the immune response. One of the best characterised involves PD-L1 (programmed cell death ligand 1), often expressed on the surface of tumour cells.

The drug does not attack the tumour. It removes the tumour's off-switch for the immune system.

Lecture 5 said the same thing from the other side

Immunodeficiency gave the evidence that immune surveillance is real: a 40× malignancy rate in transplant patients, and virally driven tumours emerging in HIV. Hallmark 8 is what a tumour must do to achieve locally what immunosuppression does systemically.

A solid tumour has every mutation needed for malignancy but stays at 2 mm. What is it missing, and why does that stop it?

Angiogenesis. A solid tumour cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm in diameter unless it has the capacity to induce angiogenesis — beyond that distance, diffusion alone cannot supply oxygen and nutrients to the centre. Growth resumes only once the balance between angiogenesis promoters and inhibitors is skewed in favour of promoters.

From the lecture slides
13

Enabling characteristics

Two things that make acquiring hallmarks easier.

Enabler 1

Genomic instability

Covered earlier — inherited or acquired loss of DNA repair, accelerating mutation accumulation. HNPCC and xeroderma pigmentosum are the inherited examples.

Enabler 2

Tumour-promoting inflammation

Inflammatory cells in the tumour microenvironment supply what the tumour needs.

What inflammation contributes

Release of factors that promote proliferation
Removal of growth suppressors
Enhanced resistance to cell death
Angiogenesis
Invasion and metastasis
Evasion of immune destruction
Read that list against the hallmarks

Inflammation supplies six of the eight hallmarks from outside the tumour cell. This is why chronic inflammation is a cancer risk — and it is the mechanistic answer to the question Lecture 6 left open about chronic candidal inflammation and epithelial dysplasia.

Clinical implication: targeted therapy

The lecture ends this section on targeted therapy. If you know which hallmark a given tumour has acquired and how, you can aim at that mechanism — a receptor, a kinase, an immune checkpoint — rather than at dividing cells in general. That is the difference between conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy and targeted agents.

14

Mechanisms of viral carcinogenesis

Three routes, one DNA and two RNA.

Virus typeMechanism
Oncogenic DNA virusViral DNA genome is integrated into host cell DNA; expression of viral oncogenes (E6 & E7) occurs; in some cases this may result in neoplastic transformation
‘Acute’ transforming RNA retrovirusAfter prior infection of a host cell, retroviral RNA combines with a transcribed RNA copy of a cellular oncogene. Reverse transcription to DNA, which integrates into the host cell genome. The RNA viral genome is then the original RNA genome + cellular oncogene (now called a viral oncogene)
‘Slow’ transforming oncogenic RNA retroviruse.g. feline leukaemia virus. Insertion of viral promoter and enhancer sequences next to a cellular oncogene, thus activating (overexpressing) it
E6 and E7 — how HPV causes cancer

The viral oncogenes named here are HPV's. E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates pRb — the two gatekeepers from Hallmark 2. The virus disables both cell-cycle checkpoints at once, without mutating either gene. That is why the lecture puts viral carcinogenesis immediately after the hallmarks: it is a worked example of acquiring Hallmark 2 by infection rather than by mutation.

Acute vs slow, in one line

An acute transforming retrovirus carries an oncogene it picked up from a previous host. A slow one carries none — it just inserts its promoter next to one of yours and turns it up. The first brings the accelerator; the second stands on the one you already had.

Every oncogenic virus from Lecture 6 fits here

HPV (oropharyngeal carcinoma), EBV (Burkitt's and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma) and HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma) are all oncogenic DNA viruses working by the first mechanism.

How does an oncogenic DNA virus produce a cancer without mutating any host gene?

Its DNA genome integrates into host cell DNA and it expresses viral oncogenes — E6 and E7. Their protein products bind and inactivate the host's tumour suppressor proteins directly: E6 inactivates p53, E7 inactivates pRb. The host genes are structurally normal; their products are neutralised. The lecture also lists this as a mechanism of p53 loss of function — binding of normal p53 to proteins encoded by oncogenic DNA viruses.

Summary and glossary

Part 2 on one screen.

The through-line

  1. Transformation is genetic and epigenetic
    Sequence changes, and changes in what gets read.
  2. Three stages
    Initiation, promotion, progression — accumulating in one clonal lineage.
  3. Brakes need two hits, accelerators need one
    Tumour suppressors recessive, oncogenes dominant — with p53's dominant-negative exception.
  4. p53 is the most mutated gene in human cancer
    Arrest in G1, or apoptosis; lost by mutation, by dominant-negative complexes, or by viral proteins.
  5. Eight hallmarks, two enablers
    And inflammation alone supplies six of the eight.
  6. Angiogenesis is the size limit
    No tumour exceeds 1–2 mm without it.
  7. Viruses take a shortcut
    E6 and E7 disable p53 and pRb without mutating them.

Glossary

Initiation
A carcinogen induces the genetic alteration(s) giving a cell its neoplastic potential.
Promotion
Stimulation of clonal proliferation of the initiated transformed cell.
Progression
The process culminating in malignant behaviour.
Clonal
Originating from a single transformed cell.
Polyclonal
Originating from multiple cells.
Carcinogen
An environmental agent participating in the causation of tumours.
Multistep carcinogenesis
The hypothesis that cancer requires successive accumulated changes.
Tumour suppressor gene
A gene whose loss removes restraint on proliferation; usually requires two hits.
Two-hit model
Both alleles of a tumour suppressor must be lost, by inheritance or acquired mutation.
Caretaker gene
Maintains genomic integrity by repairing DNA damage.
Gatekeeper gene
Inhibits proliferation or promotes death of cells with damaged DNA.
p53 / TP53
Tumour suppressor on the short arm of chromosome 17; arrests the cycle in G1 or induces apoptosis; the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer.
Dominant-negative
A mutant protein that inactivates the normal protein it complexes with — an exception to the two-hit model.
Genomic instability
Loss of the mechanisms for sensing and repairing DNA damage.
Microsatellite instability
Genomic instability from defective DNA mismatch repair, as in HNPCC.
Oncogene
A gene driving the neoplastic behaviour of cells.
Proto-oncogene
The normal cellular gene from which an oncogene arises by gain-of-function mutation.
Oncoprotein
The product of an oncogene.
Histone code
Gene regulation by histone methylation, acetylation and phosphorylation.
microRNA
Short inhibitory RNA; increased miRNA degrades mRNA and reduces expression.
Aerobic glycolysis
High glucose uptake and conversion to lactate despite ample oxygen; supplies synthetic intermediates.
Angiogenesis
New vessel formation; required for a tumour to exceed 1–2 mm.
Tropism
The preference of particular tumours for metastasis to specific tissues.
PD-L1
Programmed cell death ligand 1; an immune checkpoint often expressed on tumour cells and targeted by blocking antibodies.
E6 / E7
HPV viral oncogenes inactivating p53 and pRb respectively.
Required reading

Underwood’s Pathology: a Clinical Approach, Simon Cross (2024), Chapter 5 (Neoplasia — the section on Hallmarks of Cancer). Plus Hanahan and Weinberg 2011, Hallmarks of Cancer: The Next Generation, Cell 144(5):646–674.
